explanations.explanation: Elihu, the young man now speaking to Job, says it plainly: “My words are from an upright heart, and my lips speak sincerely what I know.” He puts that on the table before he gets into his speech. It's his own claim about himself, so keep listening to see what he does with it.

Elihu, the young man speaking to Job, doesn't point to his elders here. He says, “My words are from an upright heart, and my lips speak sincerely what I know.” So he's pointing to his own heart and what he knows.

You've got the right body part, friend, but a different adjective. Elihu, the young man speaking to Job, says, “My words are from an upright heart…” He's calling his heart upright, not troubled. A troubled heart sounds more like where Job has been living lately.

Elihu says, “Refute me if you can; prepare your case and confront me.” He's inviting Job to push back, not just nod along. That's a man who's ready for a real conversation. Honestly, I've never invited anybody to argue with my cookie recipes, so I'm a little impressed.

Elihu doesn't ask for prayer here. He says, “Refute me if you can; prepare your case and confront me.” The invitation is for Job to answer him. Praying is a fine thing to do, but it's not what this verse asks.
No waiting around in this verse. Elihu says, “Refute me if you can; prepare your case and confront me.” He wants Job to get his case ready and bring it. The text doesn't mention morning at all.

That's right. Elihu tells Job, “Surely no fear of me should terrify you; nor will my hand be heavy upon you.” He's telling Job there's no need to be afraid of him. He's saying he won't come down hard on him.

It's actually True. Elihu tells Job, “Surely no fear of me should terrify you; nor will my hand be heavy upon you.” So he tells Job not to be afraid of him. He also says his hand won't be heavy upon Job.
Elihu quotes Job saying, “Yet God finds occasions against me; He counts me as His enemy.” Those are heavy words, friend, and Elihu repeats them right back to him. Elihu is about to answer them.

Guest sounds way friendlier, but that's not the word. In Elihu's quote, Job says God “…counts me as His enemy.” That's a much sharper word than guest. Nobody gets that complaint about a dinner invitation.

I get why you'd reach for friend, because that's what you'd hope God would be called. But in the quote, Job says, “Yet God finds occasions against me; He counts me as His enemy.” Enemy is the word in the very words Elihu says he heard from Job (Job 33:8). Elihu is about to say Job isn't right in this matter (Job 33:12).
Not quite, friend. Right after those quotes, Elihu says the opposite: “Behold, you are not right in this matter.” He isn't giving Job a pat on the back. He's about to answer him.
Yes, it's False. Elihu says, “Behold, you are not right in this matter.” He doesn't agree with what he just quoted from Job. He says he's going to answer him.

Elihu says, “I will answer you, for God is greater than man.” That's the reason he gives for answering Job. It's a short sentence, but it carries the weight for everything else Elihu says here. I think of it as the top of the whole speech.

It's the other way around, friend. Elihu is the young one here, and he waited because the others were older (Job 32:4, 6). In this verse, the reason he gives is, “…for God is greater than man.” Age doesn't come up at all.
Elihu doesn't lean on Job's friends in this verse. He says, “I will answer you, for God is greater than man.” That's the reason he gives for answering. The friends don't come into it.
Elihu asks, “Why do you complain to Him that He answers nothing a man asks?” He's questioning the complaint itself. He's about to say God does speak, in one way and another (Job 33:14).

That would be a pretty strange thing to complain about, friend. Nobody grumbles that God answers everything they ask. Elihu's question is, “Why do you complain to Him that He answers nothing a man asks?” The complaint is about silence.
Close, but the word is stronger. Elihu says, “Why do you complain to Him that He answers nothing a man asks?” It's a complaint about God answering nothing at all. Elihu is about to push back on that.

explanations.answer: Through a dream or a vision
explanations.explanation: Elihu says God speaks “In a dream, in a vision in the night, when deep sleep falls upon men as they slumber on their beds…” So here the night is when God speaks. People are asleep, and that's when He opens their ears (Job 33:16).

A trumpet would certainly wake the neighborhood, friend. But Elihu doesn't mention one here. He says God speaks “In a dream, in a vision in the night, when deep sleep falls upon men…” It's a dream or vision while people sleep.

No stamps needed for this one. Elihu doesn't mention a letter. He says it's “In a dream, in a vision in the night, when deep sleep falls upon men as they slumber on their beds…” This is something that happens while people sleep.
Elihu says God sends these warnings “…to turn a man from wrongdoing and keep him from pride…” So the warnings aren't random. Elihu ties them to turning a man around. Pride is the thing he names.
Wealth is a fair guess, but it's not on the list. Elihu says the warnings are “…to turn a man from wrongdoing and keep him from pride…” Money doesn't come into the verse.

Rest might feel like the target after a night of scary warnings, friend. But Elihu says the warnings are “…to turn a man from wrongdoing and keep him from pride…” Pride is the word in the verse. Rest isn't mentioned.

It's the other way around. Elihu says the warnings are “…to preserve his soul from the Pit and his life from perishing by the sword.” The aim is to preserve the man, not end him. The Pit and the sword are the things he's kept from.
Yes, it's False. Elihu says the warnings are “…to preserve his soul from the Pit and his life from perishing by the sword.” Preserving is the goal. The warnings are about keeping him from the Pit.

That's right. Elihu says the man's pain is so bad “…that he detests his bread, and his soul loathes his favorite food.” Even the best thing on the table doesn't appeal to him. That's a rough picture of someone hurting.
It's True, friend. Elihu says the man in pain “…detests his bread, and his soul loathes his favorite food.” So even his favorite food has lost its pull. That tells you how hard the distress is.

The messenger says, “Spare him from going down to the Pit; I have found his ransom…” A ransom is the price that sets someone free. The man isn't spared because he talked his way out. Someone found the ransom for him.
That's not what the messenger finds. He says, “Spare him from going down to the Pit; I have found his ransom…” The messenger is on the man's side. He's the one who is gracious to him.

Birthright is a word from other Bible stories, friend, but not this verse. The messenger says, “Spare him from going down to the Pit; I have found his ransom…” What gets found is a ransom. That's what spares the man.
Elihu says, “…then his flesh is refreshed like a child’s; he returns to the days of his youth.” After the wasting away, his flesh is refreshed. It's a big turnaround from the Pit.
A king would be a fancy comparison, friend, but Elihu doesn't use it. He says the man's flesh “…is refreshed like a child’s; he returns to the days of his youth.” The picture is youth, not royalty.

That's a lovely picture, but it's not the one in this verse. Elihu says the man's flesh “…is refreshed like a child’s; he returns to the days of his youth.” The comparison is a child. It fits with the days of his youth.

His song says, “I have sinned and perverted what was right; yet I did not get what I deserved.” He sings it in front of people, and that takes some nerve. He doesn't hide that he sinned. He also says he didn't get what he deserved.

The song goes the other direction, friend. The man sings, “I have sinned and perverted what was right; yet I did not get what I deserved.” He owns up to his sin right out loud. Innocent isn't his claim.

explanations.answer: He had been wronged by others
explanations.explanation: He doesn't point at anyone else in this song. He sings, “I have sinned and perverted what was right; yet I did not get what I deserved.” The words are about himself. He doesn't blame other people.
Not so, friend. In his song he says, “He redeemed my soul from going down to the Pit, and I will live to see the light.” The one doing the redeeming is “He,” not “I.” The man gives the credit away.

Yes, it's False. The man sings, “He redeemed my soul from going down to the Pit, and I will live to see the light.” The song hands the redeeming to Someone else. He also looks ahead to living to see the light.

That's not what Elihu says. He says God does these things “…to bring back his soul from the Pit, that he may be enlightened with the light of life.” The reason given is bringing him back. A test of how much he can take isn't mentioned.

Yes, it's False. Elihu says God does these things “…to bring back his soul from the Pit, that he may be enlightened with the light of life.” Bringing the man back is the reason in the text. Nothing in the verse is about testing how much he can take.

Elihu says, “But if you have something to say, answer me; speak up, for I would like to vindicate you.” To vindicate is to clear someone's name. He says he'd like to do that for Job. So he leaves the door open.
Elihu doesn't say anything about testing here. He says, “But if you have something to say, answer me; speak up, for I would like to vindicate you.” To vindicate is to clear someone's name.
It's the other direction, friend. Elihu says, “speak up, for I would like to vindicate you.” To vindicate is to clear someone, not convict him. That's what Elihu says he'd like to do for Job.
